newsitem.title: USA: Hand over loot, U.S. judge tells treasure hunters.
newsitem.headline: Hand over loot, U.S. judge tells treasure hunters.

text.p: A famed family of treasure hunters must hand over the loot from a wrecked Spanish galleon and pay the U.S. government nearly $600,000 for destroying the seabed in a Florida Keys marine sanctuary, a judge has ruled.

Federal Judge Edward Davis said Kane Fisher and Salvors Inc. had salvaged treasure without permission in the Coffins Patch area of the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary and ruined more than an acre (1/2 hectare) of seagrass beds with their operating methods.
In a ruling given in chambers on Wednesday and obtained by Reuters on Thursday, Davis ordered them to pay $589,311 for a restoration project and to cover damage assessment costs.
They must also hand over booty including silver coins, plates and forks, gold bullion and iron cannon from the galleon San Fernando, which sank in a hurricane in 1773.

The case was the first brought by the government over environmental damage to the sanctuary, which covers a 2,800 square nautical mile area of coral reef, seagrass and mangrove shoreline in the Florida Keys.

Kane Fisher and his father, legendary treasure hunter Mel Fisher, mounted a salvage operation in Coffins Patch in 1992. Working off three boats, they blew holes in the seabed using L-shaped pipes of Fisher's own design that used the powerful wash of propellers to blast the sea bed and uncover artifacts.
The government said they gouged out more than 600 craters, averaging three to five feet (one to 1.6 m) deep and 20 to 30 feet wide (7.5 to 10 m), over a 1.6 acre (6,470 sq.m) area.
Divers and sanctuary officials who testified in the case said they saw clumps of uprooted seagrass the size of hay bales lying in the blow-holes.

Environmental biologist Curtis Kruer said the only similar damage he had seen was from bombs dropped from airplanes on a test range in waters near Puerto Rico. Experts said tbe grasses would take between 50 and 100 years to grow back.

The Fishers' lawyers had argued the grasses could grow back in just a few years and that some of the holes were made by earlier treasure hunters. The Fishers also maintained that the treasure was rightfully theirs because the galleon had sunk before the United States existed.
Pat Klyne, a spokesman for Salvors, said the ruling heralded a government campaign to close down salvagers.

"NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) wants to go treasure hunting itself and we're going to be paying for it. Plus they get what we've already found," he told Reuters by telephone from Key West.
"It confirms our worst fears. I guess it's a case of 'He's the world's greatest treasure hunter -- let's dethrone him.'"
He repeated the Fishers' position that the area had been worked by salvagers for more than 30 years and that the damaged area was far less than stated by the government.
The judge's ruling said the purpose of sanctuaries "is to preserve sensitive areas for their conservation, recreational, ecological or esthetic value."
The recovered artifacts were "a sanctuary resource ... that contribute to the historical value of the sanctuary," it said.
Mel Fisher was originally named in the suit but was removed after Kane said his father was too ill from chemotherapy to know much about the 1992 expedition.

The senior Fisher, who is based in Key West, earned fame and fortune when he found the galleon Nuestra Senora de Atocha off the Keys and brought up a trove of treasure in the 1980s. He fought and won a long battle with the government to keep the Atocha treasure, some of which is on display in Key West.
